1212.title: The peace churches
1212.hook: Mennonites, Quakers and Brethren refuse to fight, following Matthew 5:39
1212.howItsDone: Mennonite, Quaker and Brethren congregations teach nonviolence as part of following Jesus; members have sought to serve as conscientious objectors rather than bear arms, and these churches run relief, rebuilding and peacemaking work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, just war: Augustine and Aquinas drawing a fence around fighting. Your line was war has limits.

A young man stands in front of a draft board with a Bible under his arm. He isn't dodging hard work. He'll drive an ambulance, fight forest fires, empty bedpans on a hospital ward. The one thing he won't do is carry a rifle. When they ask him why, he opens to the Sermon on the Mount and reads a single sentence out loud. Yesterday, Christians who say a war can be just, inside strict limits. Today, the Christians who answer: not for us. Mennonites, Quakers, the Brethren. The peace churches.

The sentence is Matthew 5:39: "But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also." The peace churches take that as plain instruction for ordinary life, with no exception carved out for war. They point to the night Jesus was arrested. One of his followers draws a sword, and Jesus answers with yesterday's line, which the peace churches read as a rule for their own lives: "Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword." Then he walks toward the cross without a fight. Now notice what turning the cheek is not. It isn't running away, and it isn't shrugging. The person who turns the other cheek is still standing there, face to face. Paul puts it in one line: "Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good." So the peace churches pair the refusal with action: relief work after floods and wars, rebuilding houses, sitting between two sides of a quarrel. Quakers call their stance a testimony, something a life says out loud. Christians in the just war tradition read the same sermon and conclude that protecting the weak can sometimes require force. This path won't rank them. Each side hands the other a hard question: who protects the neighbor, and what does it cost to turn the cheek? And both hear the same sermon go on: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you."

Bring to mind one little conflict you're in right now, a sharp text thread, a roommate, a sibling, and notice the move you'd usually make to win it. Then picture the peace churches' way: staying there, not striking back and not walking off, and doing one good thing instead, a softer answer, a real question. If you pray, you can hold that person before God.
The peace churches. Mennonites, Quakers and Brethren, who read turn the other cheek as a word for all of life, and refuse to fight while working for peace.
Your line: the peaceable way. Not running, not striking: still standing there. That's today, done.

1213.title: Earn, save, give
1213.hook: Wesley's sermon on money: gain all you can honestly, save all you can, give all you can
1213.howItsDone: Methodists and other Christians still teach from Wesley's sermon The Use of Money; churches often use it in teaching on stewardship, budgeting and giving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the peace churches: Mennonites, Quakers and Brethren, who refuse to fight and answer evil with good. Your line was the peaceable way.

A paycheck lands on a Friday. Before a cent of it is spent, its owner has already sorted it: rent, the car, groceries, that thing in the online cart, and maybe, if anything is left, something for somebody else. John Wesley, the preacher whose followers became the Methodists, wrote a sermon about exactly that moment, called The Use of Money. Preachers are sometimes expected to treat money as a danger to keep at arm's length. Wesley didn't. He told his listeners to go out and earn.

Wesley's sermon gives money three rules, in order. First, gain all you can, but honestly, and with limits: not by work that wrecks your own health, not by hurting your neighbor, their body, their business or their soul. Earning, for Wesley, was part of faithfulness, as long as nobody paid for it with harm. Second, save all you can. And here's the surprise: by save, Wesley didn't mean stockpile. He meant cut the waste. Don't throw money at showing off, at things bought to be admired, at feeding every craving. Saving kept money free for something better. Third, give all you can. That's where the first two were heading the whole time. In his telling, someone who earns hard and saves hard but stops there has missed the point and only built a bigger pile. Wesley wasn't inventing this. Paul tells a reformed thief in Ephesians to work with his hands, and gives the reason: "that he may have to give to him that needeth." Earning, there, points outward from the start. Paul also warns Timothy that "the love of money is the root of all evil." Notice the word: the love of it, not the money itself. Wesley's three rules are one way of keeping the money and losing the love. Earn so you have something. Save so it isn't wasted. Give, because that was what it was for.

Think back over the last week of spending and find one small thing you didn't really need, a delivery fee, a second coffee, an impulse buy: that amount is saved money in Wesley's sense, waste you could cut. Now ask where it could go instead, a neighbor, a food bank, a friend who's short this month, a cause you already trust. If you pray, you can ask for a generous heart.
Earn. In Wesley's sermon, the first of three rules for money: gain all you can, honestly, without harm, so that you have something to save and to give.
Your line: give all you can. The pile was never the point. See you tomorrow.

1214.title: The milkmaid's vocation
1214.hook: Luther said a milkmaid's work pleases God as much as a monk's
1214.howItsDone: Lutheran and other Protestant churches teach the doctrine of vocation, that ordinary work and family life are callings from God; Catholic teaching also speaks of the vocation of lay people in the world, and some churches bless workers and their tools.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Wesley's three rules for money: earn honestly, save by cutting waste, then give. Your line was give all you can.

Before dawn, in a cold barn, a young woman sits on a stool with her cheek against a cow's warm side, and the milk rings into the pail. Up the hill, in a monastery, a monk is already at prayer in the chapel. Ask the village which of the two is doing holy work, and the answer comes fast. Martin Luther gave a different answer, and it startled people. Christians still repeat a saying credited to him: the milkmaid's work, done in faith, pleases God as much as the monk's.

A vocation is a calling. In the world Luther grew up in, the word had come to belong to one kind of life: priests, monks and nuns. They had a calling; everyone else simply had a job. Luther pushed back hard. He argued that God calls the farmer, the parent, the shoemaker and the servant girl just as truly, and that their work serves God by serving neighbors. The baby gets fed. The town has shoes. The bread arrives. He leaned on Paul's advice to the Corinthians: "Let every man abide in the same calling wherein he was called." Your ordinary station is where faith gets lived. Paul says it another way in Colossians, writing to people who were servants: "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men." Notice who that was written to. Not preachers. People doing someone else's chores. This idea took root in the churches that came from Luther, and it isn't only theirs: Catholic teaching today also speaks of the vocation of lay people, and of work as a share in God's own work. Luther, a former monk himself, never stopped praying. What he argued against was the idea that a monk's vows earned more with God than a farmer's faith. He refused a ladder, with spiritual jobs at the top and the barn at the bottom. Diapers, spreadsheets, a cash register: in this view, they can be a calling too.
screen: `DO IT HEARTILY, AS TO THE LORD.`

1215.title: Sabbath economics
1215.hook: rest, gleaning and jubilee limit greed
1215.howItsDone: Some Christians and churches take up Sabbath economics through practices like a weekly day without shopping, food gleaning projects that gather leftover crops for the poor, and jubilee campaigns for debt relief.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the milkmaid's vocation: Luther's claim that the barn can be as holy as the chapel. Your line was every job is holy.

Harvest time in ancient Israel. A farmer walks the edge of his barley field with a sickle, and right where he could take the last good rows, he stops. The corners stay standing. The stalks his workers dropped stay on the ground. Later, a widow and a stranger from out of town walk in behind them and gather what was left, and nobody chases them off. The farmer isn't being sloppy, and he isn't being nice. He's obeying the law. The Bible builds limits right into the economy.

It starts with a day. The commandment in Exodus gives six days for work and the seventh for rest, and it spells out who rests: not only the family, but the servants, the animals and the stranger too. Deuteronomy repeats the commandment and adds a reason: the rest is given "that thy manservant and thy maidservant may rest as well as thou." And then: "remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt." A people who remember being servants are told to let their own servants rest. Rest isn't a reward for the people at the top. Everyone gets it. Then the harvest law in Leviticus: "thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field, neither shalt thou gather the gleanings of thy harvest." Those are left, the text says, for the poor and the stranger. And then the boldest one, jubilee. Leviticus describes a fiftieth year when land returns to the families who first held it, and the trumpet tells the people to "proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof." Leviticus doesn't say whether the jubilee was ever fully kept. But the idea is plain: nobody's gain is meant to swallow a neighbor forever, because, as God says in the same chapter, "the land is mine." The manna story from earlier in this stretch belongs to the same family: bread that spoiled when it was hoarded. Christians who speak of Sabbath economics read all of these together: rest, gleaning, release. Each one puts a fence around greed. Each one says there is enough, if nobody takes it all.

Picture a day with no purchases at all, no tapping a card, no cart, no quick snack on the way home, and notice which purchase is hardest to imagine skipping. Then picture what you already have: food in the cupboard, clothes on the hook, a roof. If you pray, you can give thanks for what's already in the house.
Sabbath economics. The Bible's limits on greed, read together: rest for everyone, servants included, corners left for the poor, and a jubilee of release.
Your line: enough for all. The corners of the field were left for others. Until next time.

1216.title: Marriage
1216.hook: for some churches a sacrament, for others a covenant; all see it as faithful love
1216.howItsDone: Christians marry in church services with vows exchanged before God and witnesses; Catholic and Orthodox churches celebrate marriage as a sacrament, while Protestant churches celebrate it as a covenant or holy estate blessed by God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sabbath economics: rest for everyone, corners of the field left standing, a jubilee of release. Your line was enough for all.

Two people stand at the front of a church, hands joined, a little nervous. The words they repeat are old. In the Book of Common Prayer, the groom promises: "to have and to hold from this day forward, for better for worse, for richer for poorer, in sickness and in health, to love and to cherish, till death us do part." The bride's promise runs almost word for word the same. Nobody in the room knows which of those they'll get. That's the point. They promise all of it, in advance. Christians in quite different churches make promises like these, even when they explain them in different words.

The root is in the opening pages of Genesis: "Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh." Leave, cleave, become one. When Jesus is asked about divorce, he goes straight back to that verse and adds a line still heard at weddings: "What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder." So for him, marriage isn't only a private contract. God is the one joining. Here churches describe it differently. Catholic and Orthodox Christians count marriage as a sacrament: a holy sign through which God's grace is truly given to the couple. In the Catholic understanding, the bride and groom are the ministers of the sacrament to each other. Lutheran and Reformed churches don't number marriage among the sacraments. They call it a covenant, or a holy estate that God created and blesses: a promise made before God and witnesses, with God as a party to it. Paul, writing to the Ephesians about husbands and wives, says: "This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church." That one line holds the common ground. Whatever word a church uses, sacrament or covenant, they agree that a faithful marriage is meant to show something about God: love that chooses the other person again, for better and for worse, and doesn't leave.

Choose a couple you know, your parents, grandparents, friends, neighbors, or your own marriage if you have one, and picture them on an ordinary day, not the wedding day: somebody's tired, somebody's doing dishes. Which of the old vows are they living right now? If you pray, you can pray for them by name; if you don't, just wish them well, specifically.
Marriage. For Catholic and Orthodox Christians, a sacrament; for Lutheran and Reformed churches, among others, a covenant before God. For both, faithful love: two becoming one flesh.
Your line: two becoming one. For better, for worse, chosen again. Until tomorrow.

1217.title: Singleness
1217.hook: Paul and Jesus were single; celibacy is honored as a calling
1217.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox monks and nuns take vows of celibacy, and Latin-rite Catholic priests are ordinarily celibate; Christians across churches also honor single believers who serve in congregations, missions and communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, marriage: a sacrament for some churches, a covenant for others, faithful love for all of them. Your line was two becoming one.

A wedding reception, table nine. The single friend gets the question again, from an aunt, kindly meant: so when's it your turn? Everyone laughs. The friend laughs too, a half second late. Here's something that might surprise that aunt. The Gospels never mention a wife for Jesus. And Paul tells the Corinthians he wishes more people could live as he does: unmarried. Two figures at the heart of the Christian story, and neither one is shown at a wedding of his own.

Start with Paul's own words to the Corinthians: "For I would that all men were even as I myself. But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that." Notice the word gift. Paul isn't saying single people are waiting for real life to begin, and he isn't saying married people have settled for less. Each way of life is a gift, and each person has their own. He even gives a practical reason: the unmarried person can give undivided attention to the things of the Lord. Jesus speaks of some who give up marriage for the kingdom of heaven's sake, and adds, he that is able to receive it, let him receive it. Not everyone, then. But some, as a calling. Christians have honored that calling in different ways. Catholic and Orthodox monks and nuns make vows of celibacy. In the Latin Catholic church, priests are ordinarily celibate; Orthodox priests may marry before they are ordained, though their bishops are chosen from the celibate. Protestant churches don't require celibacy of their ministers, and they too honor single believers who serve with their whole lives. And there's an older promise still, from Isaiah, to those who would never have children: "Even unto them will I give in mine house and within my walls a place and a name better than of sons and of daughters." A place and a name. Not someday, after a wedding. Already. A single life, in this reading, isn't half of something.

Bring to mind someone in your life who is single, by choice, by circumstance, after loss, or simply not yet, and set aside every question about their dating life. Look instead at what their life already holds, their work, the people they show up for, and name one thing clearly; if you're the single one, turn this toward yourself. If you pray, you can give thanks for them.
Singleness. In Paul's words, a gift from God like marriage is a gift, and for some, a calling to serve with an undivided heart.
Your line: whole already. A gift, in Paul's word, not a waiting room. See you tomorrow.

1218.title: Where churches disagree today
1218.hook: on sexuality and gender, churches reach sincerely different conclusions; the path won't rank them
1218.howItsDone: Churches discuss questions of sexuality and gender in synods, conventions, councils and congregational meetings; some have reaffirmed traditional teaching, some have changed their practice, and some allow congregations to differ.

segments.voice: Yesterday, singleness: Paul calling it a gift, and Isaiah's promise of a place and a name. Your line was whole already.

Thanksgiving dinner. Two cousins, raised in the same church, both still praying, both reading the same Bible. Somebody mentions a wedding, and the table goes quiet, because the cousins have landed in different places on a question about sexuality, and each got there by praying and reading. Neither one is faking. This week has walked through peace and war, money, work, marriage and singleness. It ends at a place where churches feel strain. On sexuality and gender, Christians reach sincerely different conclusions. This path won't rank them.

Here's the shape of it, as fairly as it can be put. Some churches teach that marriage is between a man and a woman, and that sex belongs inside it. They point to Genesis, to Jesus quoting Genesis on marriage, and to passages in Paul, and they hold that the church should keep teaching what it has received, while saying that everyone is welcome to come and worship. Other churches bless same-sex marriages and open every part of church life, including leadership, to gay and transgender members. They also point to scripture: to Jesus welcoming those others pushed to the edge, and to times the early church changed course, like the decision in Acts to welcome Gentiles without requiring circumcision. Some people sit somewhere between, or are still unsure. Both sides are reading the Bible. Both are trying to be faithful. These questions have split denominations and strained families, and the hurt runs on more than one side. So what does the tradition offer for the disagreement itself? Paul, writing to a church divided over food and holy days, said: "Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another." To the Ephesians he wrote of "speaking the truth in love." Both halves count: truth as each side sees it, and love that doesn't leave the table. And Jesus named a mark that should still show through any argument: "By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another." Not if you agree. If you love.
